'''''Mastocarpus stellatus''''', commonly known as '''carrageenan moss''' or '''false Irish moss''',<ref>{{cite web |title=False Irish moss (Mastocarpus stellatus) - MarLIN - The Marine Life Information Network |url=https://www.marlin.ac.uk/species/detail/1446 |website=www.marlin.ac.uk}}</ref><ref name=":33">{{Cite journal|date=2014-10-01|title=Integral Mastocarpus stellatus use for antioxidant edible film development|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0268005X14000629|journal=Food Hydrocolloids|language=en|volume=40|pages=128–137|doi=10.1016/j.foodhyd.2014.02.013|issn=0268-005X|last1=Blanco-Pascual|first1=N.|last2=Gómez-Guillén|first2=M.C.|last3=Montero|first3=M.P.|url-access=subscription}}</ref> is a species in the [[Rhodophyceae]] division, a red algae seaweed division, and the [[Phyllophoraceae|Phyllophoracea]] family. ''M. stellatus'' is closely related to [[Chondrus crispus|Irish Moss]] (''Chondrus crispus''). It grows in the [[intertidal zone]]. It is most collected in North Atlantic regions such as [[Ireland]] and [[Scotland]], together with Irish moss, dried, and sold for cooking and as the basis for a drink reputed to ward off colds and flu. Marine biologists have completed studies on the medicinal reputation of ''M. stellatus'' to discover the full potential of its pharmaceutical benefits. Additionally, marine biologists have conducted research on its potential to serve as an alternative to plastic. The application of ''M. stellatus'' in these different industries is correlated with the seaweed's adaptations which developed in response to the environmental stressors present around its location on the rocky intertidal.
[[File:Mastocarpus stellatus 19880601a.jpg|alt=Mastocarpus stellatus|thumb|226x226px|''Mastocarpus stellatus'' removed from the rocky intertidal]]

== Description ==
It grows from a discoid holdfast [[Stipe (botany)|stipe]], and the [[fronds]] are channeled unlike those of ''[[Chondrus crispus]],'' which are flat. It grows to a height of {{Convert|10-20|cm|in|abbr=on}} and branches dichotomously. The frond is cartilaginous and reddish-brown in colour, with a greenish or purplish tinge. The mature algae show reproductive structures which develop on erect filaments up to {{Convert|1|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter, these make it readily distinguishable from ''Chondrus crispus''. In colour it is reddish brown, purple or bleached.<ref>Newton, L. 1931. ''A Handbook of the British Seaweeds''. British Museum</ref><ref name="Dixon 772">Dixon, P.S. & M. Irvine. 1977. ''Seaweeds of the British Isles. Volume 1 Rhodophyta pt.1''. British Museum (Natural History), London. {{ISBN|0 565 00781 5}}</ref>

== Ecology ==

=== Habitat and distribution ===
''M. stellatus'' occurs commonly on rocks in the mid and lower-intertidal. It is generally found on all coasts of [[Ireland]] and [[Great Britain|Britain]], except perhaps for parts of the east of England: [[Lincoln, Lincolnshire|Lincoln]], [[Norfolk]] and [[Suffolk]].<ref name="Hardy and Guiry 062">'''Hardy, F.G. and Guiry, M.D.''' 2006. ''A Check-list and Atlas of the Seaweeds of Britain and Ireland.''. The British Phycological Society. {{ISBN|3-906166-35-X}}</ref> Other recorded locations include: [[Iceland]], [[Faeroes]], [[North Russia]] to [[Río de Oro|Rio de Oro]], [[Canada]] (Newfoundland) to [[United States|U.S.]] (North Carolina).<ref name="Dixon 772"/> ''Mastocarpus stellatus'' is able to coexist with ''C. crispus'' on the northern New England coast despite being a competitive inferior to ''C. crispus''.  A greater tolerance for freezing allows it to exist above ''C. crispus'' in northern environments where freezing stresses are significant.  ''M. stellatus'' is rarely found south of [[Cape Cod]] on the [[United States]] [[East Coast of the United States|Atlantic coast]] because it is out competed by ''C. crispus'' when the freezing tolerances are lower.{{Citation needed|date=September 2021}}

=== Evolutionary adaptations ===
''M. stellatus'' is morphologically similar to ''Chondrus crispus''. Both species endure high levels of environmental stress from freezing temperatures, [[desiccation]], high light, and hyper or hypo-[[osmotic shock]]. The degree of stress placed on the algae by these factors varies depending on the time of year and latitude. These stressors result in the production of [[Reactive oxygen species|reactive oxygen]]; large amounts of reactive oxygen around the algae can damage the organisms’ DNA, proteins, and lipids.<ref name=":0">Collén, J., & Davison, I. R. (1999). Stress tolerance and reactive oxygen metabolism in the intertidal red seaweeds Mastocarpus stellatus and Chondrus crispus. ''Plant, Cell & Environment'', ''22''(9), 1143–1151. {{doi|10.1046/j.1365-3040.1999.00477.x}}</ref>

To defend against excessive production of reactive oxygen, these organisms use [[antioxidant]]s to reduce oxygen levels. Compared to ''C. crispus'', ''M. stellatus''’ location on the rocky [[Intertidal zone|intertidal]] experiences greater fluctuations in environmental stressors. ''M. stellatus'' was found to have higher levels of oxygen metabolism and a faster decomposition rate than ''C. crispus''. Additionally, ''M. stellatus'' makes use of scavenging [[enzyme]]s including: [[catalase]], [[superoxide dismutase]], [[glutathione reductase]], and [[ascorbate peroxidase]] (to scavenge [[hydrogen peroxide]]). After conducting his research on ''M. stellatus'' and ''C. crispus'' in 1999, Jonas Collén argued that the difference between the species may be an evolutionary adaptation by adopting different strategies to cope with environmental stressors at differing intertidal zones and locations.<ref name=":0" /> ''M. stellatus'' showed responses to changes to tidal height with changes in oxygen metabolism, suggesting that the increase in this enzyme activity (which produces a higher content of soluble protein to break down reactive oxygen compounds) requires energy allocation to these enzymes in order to adapt stress tolerance.<ref name=":0" />

== Reproduction and life history ==
In 1979, [[Michael D. Guiry|Michael Guiry]] and John A. West conducted a study and determined that ''M. stellatus'' exhibits two distinct [[biological life cycle]]s and reproduction processes; the first type being heteromorphic and the second being direct.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Guiry|first1=M. D.|last2=West|first2=J. A.|last3=Kim|first3=D.-H.|last4=Masuda|first4=M.|date=1984|title=Reinstatement of the Genus Mastocarpus Kützing (Rhodophyta)|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1222029|journal=Taxon|volume=33|issue=1|pages=53–63|doi=10.2307/1222029|jstor=1222029|issn=0040-0262|url-access=subscription}}</ref> ''M. stellatuses'' exhibiting the heteromorphic-type life history are [[dioecious]] plants (in a broad sense) that reproduce sexually by alternating [[diploid]] crustose [[Tetrasporaphyte|tetrasporophytes]] with foliose [[gametophyte]]s. ''M. stellatus'' that have direct-type life histories reproduce asexually because fertilization never occurred. This results in the production of [[carpospore]]s by the female gametophytes, resulting in the growth of foliose plants that lack [[tetrasporangia]].<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal|last1=Dudgeon|first1=Steve|last2=Kübler|first2=Janet E.|last3=West|first3=John A.|last4=Kamiya|first4=Mitsunobu|last5=Krueger-Hadfield|first5=Stacy A.|date=2017-05-01|title=Asexuality and the cryptic species problem|url=https://www.schweizerbart.de/papers/pip/detail/4/87244/Asexuality_and_the_cryptic_species_problem|journal=Perspectives in Phycology|volume=4|language=en|pages=47–59|doi=10.1127/pip/2017/0070|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Tetrasporangia are pivotal in sexual reproduction because, through [[meiosis]], they create four unique tetraspores as male or female [[gamete]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mikami|first1=Koji|last2=Li|first2=Chengze|last3=Irie|first3=Ryunosuke|last4=Hama|first4=Yoichiro|date=2019-08-07|title=A unique life cycle transition in the red seaweed Pyropia yezoensis depends on apospory|journal=Communications Biology|language=en|volume=2|issue=1|page=299|doi=10.1038/s42003-019-0549-5|pmid=31396579|pmc=6685973|issn=2399-3642|doi-access=free}}</ref> Since ''M. stellatus'' that produce asexually do not develop tetrasporangia, they are "genetically isolated" from sexually producing ''M. stellatus''.<ref name=":12" />

== Modern uses ==
The earliest record of collecting Irish seaweed is evidenced by 12th century poems by monks, according to Michael Guiry. In a 2001 market analysis of Irish seaweed aquaculture, the estimated combined annual national seaweed harvest of ''M. stellatus'' and ''C. crispus'' was less than 100 tonnes.<ref name=":02">Walsh, M., Watson, L., Robinson, G., Maggs, C., & Edwards, M. (2001). ''[https://www.seaweed.ie/irish_seaweed_contacts/doc/A%20Market%20Analysis%20towards%20the%20Further%20Development%20of%20Seaweed%20Aquaculture%20in%20Ireland.pdf Part 1 A Market Analysis towards the Further Development of Seaweed Aquaculture in Ireland.]'' 52.</ref> ''M. stellatus''  is harvested during the [[gametophyte]] life phase because later phases, with more sulphated [[carrageenan]], are harder to remove from its rock. The food and pharmaceutical industries are interested in the seaweed for their antioxidant, [[anticoagulant]], and thickening or gelling properties. Antioxidant and anticoagulant properties are determined by sulfation, molecular weight, location of sulfate groups, sugar composition, and glycosidic branching.<ref name=":1" /> In addition to its health properties and applications, the gelling properties of ''M. stellatus'' can create a [[biodegradable]] film that may be a sustainable and edible alternative to plastics for food preservation and functional food development.<ref name=":33"/>

=== Alternative to plastic ===
Carrageen is the active [[polysaccharide]] compound that is responsible for the mechanisms that give the plant its antioxidant, anticoagulant, and gelling properties. The process of extracting the carrageenan from the ''M. stellatus'' usually consists of boiling the plant for several hours and using ethanolic precipitation to isolate the compound. Researchers found that the concentration of carrageen substance and efficiency of properties is dependent on the extraction conditions including boiling temperatures, drying methods, and dilution techniques. These compounds were used to create films to determine how chemical structures and biological reactions can be manipulated to produce beneficial levels of elasticity, durability, solubility, water resistance, and thickness required for an effective alternative to [[food packaging]].<ref name=":33"/> Their findings suggest that higher concentrations of sulfate and proteins in the carrageenan reinforces the molecular structure, increases thickness, increases elasticity, and prevents water filtration, making the gel stronger. However, the strength between these bonds causes a concentration of force at their intersection which makes it easier to break. More studies must be conducted to test for more factors of ''M. stellatus'' and degrees of property efficacy.<ref name=":33" />

=== Medicinal supplement ===
Carrageenan, or [[phycocolloid]]s are sulfated linear polysaccharides composed of carrageenan and carrageenan precursors. In order for carrageenan compounds to be useful, the kappa and/or iota carrageenan need to be isolated from its mu-carrageenan or nu-carrageenan precursors.<ref name=":33"/>{{Technical inline|date=September 2021}}  Lower molecular weight and higher amounts of sulfate results in higher antioxidant properties. Heavier molecular weight and higher amounts of sulfate result in anticoagulant properties. The relationships between antioxidant and anticoagulant mechanisms suggest that inflammation and [[coagulation]] are interconnected and interdependent processes in ''M. stellatus''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|date=2014-01-01|title=Bioactivity of sulfated polysaccharides from the edible red seaweed Mastocarpus stellatus|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2212619814000035|journal=Bioactive Carbohydrates and Dietary Fibre|language=en|volume=3|issue=1|pages=29–40|doi=10.1016/j.bcdf.2014.01.002|issn=2212-6198|last1=Gómez-Ordóñez|first1=Eva|last2=Jiménez-Escrig|first2=Antonio|last3=Rupérez|first3=Pilar|url-access=subscription}}</ref> ''M. stellatus'' has been used in home remedies to treat coughs, colds, and sore throats by mixing it with ''C. crispus'' and other herbs, spices, and sweeteners.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2018-11-15|title=Carrageen Seaweed Cough and Cold Syrup|url=http://www.wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/carrageen-seaweed-cough-and-cold-syrup/|access-date=2021-04-17|website=Wild Walks Southwest|language=en-GB}}</ref>
